issues.legal_issue: A state levy calculated on royalties from mining lands is not a tax on land, land revenue, or mineral rights, and cannot be sustained as a fee where it lacks a service nexus and intrudes into the field of Union control over mineral development.
material_facts: The levy on mining lands was calculated by reference to royalty or dead rent, with rates expressed as percentages or multiples of those amounts, and the cess was assessed and collected along with royalty or dead rent.
The levy’s treatment of mining lands had been separated from other lands, and the method and scale of calculation showed that royalty, rather than land as a unit, was the subject of the levy.
Only part of the proceeds was earmarked for specified purposes, and the earmarking did not relate services to the mining operators who paid the levy.
The parliamentary mining legislation provided for regulation of mineral development and addressed royalties, dead rent, fees, and related matters.
issues.conclusion: The levy under the relevant state cess legislation was beyond the competence of the State Legislature and was unconstitutional.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 246 and 265 and Entries 45, 49, 50, 23 and 66 of List II, read with Entry 54 of List I, a tax on royalty is not thereby a tax on land or land revenue; a tax on royalty is not a tax on minerals or mineral rights for purposes of Entry 50. A tax on land must be directly imposed on land as a unit and bear a direct relationship to it. A fee must relate to services rendered or to be rendered to the class paying it and must concern a matter within the State List. Where Parliament has declared mineral regulation and development expedient in the public interest, the extent to which the central enactment occupies that field determines the erosion of State legislative power. The Court followed India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu, Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, and State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co.; it explained that the land-tax reasoning in H.R.S. Murthy v. Collector of Chittoor could not sustain the levy after India Cement. It also relied on the principles in Ajay Kumar Mukherjea v. Local Board of Barpeta, Ralla Ram v. Province of East Punjab, Buxa Dooars Tea Co. v. State, and Union of India v. Bombay Tyre International.

rule.if: state_cess_validity_challenge and mining_cess_tracks_royalty and cess_is_collected_with_royalty and (not services_are_correlated_to_mining_payers or central_mining_control_covers_the_field)

predicates.state_cess_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state-imposed cess on mining activity.
predicates.mining_cess_tracks_royalty: The cess on mining lands is calculated by reference to royalty or dead rent rather than directly on land as a unit.
predicates.cess_is_collected_with_royalty: The state assesses or collects the cess together with royalty or dead rent.
predicates.services_are_correlated_to_mining_payers: The state earmarks the proceeds for services connected to the class of mining operators who pay the cess.
predicates.central_mining_control_covers_the_field: A central legal regime controls mineral development and covers the subject matter of the state levy.

issues.definition: When a challenged state cess on mining activity tracks royalty and is either unconnected to services for its payers or within a field controlled by the Union, the levy is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A cess levied directly on royalties from mines and quarries cannot be sustained as a tax on land or mineral rights, as a fee without an adequate service basis, or as a pre-constitutional levy preserved despite later parliamentary control of the field.
material_facts: The statute specifically assessed cess on royalties from mines and quarries, and notifications set the levy as a percentage or multiple of royalty.
The statute directed some proceeds to district funds and the remainder to the State’s consolidated fund for public works, while also requiring a portion to be spent on mineral development.
The levy at issue operated under amended statutory provisions enacted after the Constitution came into force.
issues.conclusion: The levy under the Bengal Cess Act, as applicable in the State, was invalid; Article 277 did not preserve it.
issues.legal_principle: Entries 45, 49 and 50 of List II do not authorize a levy that is in substance imposed directly on royalties; a partial allocation of proceeds to public or mineral-development purposes does not, without the necessary service relationship, establish a valid fee. Article 277 preserves only qualifying taxes, duties, cesses or fees lawfully levied immediately before the Constitution and continued for the same purposes until Parliament provides otherwise. The Court applied India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu and the principles concerning Article 277 in Ramkrishna Ramanath v. Janpad Sabha and Town Municipal Committee v. Ramachandra.

predicates.state_cess_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state cess on mining activity.
predicates.cess_is_directly_assessed_on_royalty: The statute or its implementing measures calculate the cess directly as a percentage or multiple of royalty from mines or quarries.
predicates.proceeds_are_not_a_correlated_service_fe: The proceeds are not shown to fund services correlated to the class of persons paying the cess.
predicates.levy_is_not_a_continuation_for_the_same_: The challenged levy was enacted or materially changed after the Constitution, or it does not continue the same levy for the same purposes.

issues.definition: A challenged state cess directly assessed on mining royalties is unconstitutional when it is not a correlated service fee or does not qualify as a continuing levy for the same purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A cess imposed per unit of major mineral raised, rather than on land or mineral rights, is not authorized as a tax on land or mineral rights.
material_facts: The statute imposed the cess per ton of major mineral raised from land held in connection with mineral rights.
The liability depended on minerals being raised and was not determined by the area or value of the land.
issues.conclusion: The levy under the relevant part of the state upkar legislation was ultra vires because it was not covered by Entry 49 or Entry 50 of List II.
issues.legal_principle: The constitutional character of a tax depends on its substance, not its form. A levy whose subject is the quantity of mineral produced is not a tax on land under Entry 49 or a tax on mineral rights under Entry 50. The Court approved the reasoning in M.P. Lime Manufacturers’ Association v. State and applied the principles in India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu and Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa.

predicates.state_cess_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state cess connected with mining.
predicates.cess_is_charged_per_unit_of_mineral_rais: The state charges the cess according to the quantity of mineral produced or raised.
predicates.liability_does_not_depend_on_land_area_o: The liability does not depend on the area or value of the land and arises from mineral production.

issues.definition: A challenged state cess charged per unit of mineral produced, with liability independent of land area or value, is unconstitutional as a tax on land or mineral rights.

issues.legal_issue: A levy earmarked for development of mineral-bearing areas may be a fee, but it is outside State legislative competence when it concerns mineral development in a field occupied by parliamentary legislation.
material_facts: The statute imposed a cess on land held under a mining lease and set its measure by reference to royalty or dead rent.
The proceeds were expressly directed toward development of mineral-bearing areas, supporting treatment of the levy as a fee.
The parliamentary mining legislation declared Union control over mineral development and covered the relevant field.
issues.conclusion: The mineral-areas development cess was invalid because, although it could be treated as a fee, its subject matter fell within the field occupied by parliamentary legislation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Entries 23 and 66 of List II, a fee must concern a matter within the State List. Entry 23 is subject to Union legislation under Entry 54 of List I. A declaration under Entry 54 erodes State competence to the extent of the field assumed by Parliament, assessed by considering the central enactment and matters legitimately within its scope. The Court relied on the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, including sections 2, 9, 9A, 13, 18 and 25, and followed Hingir-Rampur Coal Co. Ltd. v. State of Orissa, State of Orissa v. M.A. Tulloch & Co., and India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu. It also considered Srinivasa Traders v. State.

predicates.state_cess_validity_challenge: A party challenges the constitutional validity of a state levy connected with mining.
predicates.levy_is_earmarked_for_mineral_area_devel: The state directs the proceeds of the levy toward development of mineral-bearing areas.
predicates.central_mining_control_covers_the_field: A central legal regime controls mineral development and covers the subject matter of the state levy.

issues.definition: A state levy earmarked for mineral-area development is outside State competence when central control covers that field.

issues.legal_issue: A declaration that a tax levy is unconstitutional does not automatically entitle the payer to a refund of all amounts collected before the declaration.
material_facts: The Court held the challenged cess levies unconstitutional, and the assessees sought refunds of sums collected before the relevant judgments declaring the levies invalid.
The levies had been collected over time, and the States relied on the prior legal position and the consequences that repayment of all earlier collections would have for State interests and finances.

The Court directed refunds only for collections made on or after the relevant judgment declaring the levy unconstitutional, with interest; where an intermediary had collected the cess, it was to pass the refund to its customers.
issues.conclusion: Refund was not automatic: no refund was directed for collections before the relevant declaration of invalidity, while post-declaration collections were to be refunded with interest.
issues.legal_principle: The declaration that a levy is invalid and the relief granted as a consequence are distinct; a court has discretion to grant, withhold, or restrict relief to advance justice. In writ proceedings, delay, laches, third-party rights, unjust enrichment, and vital State interests may be relevant, and invalidity does not compel repayment of every earlier collection. The Court followed India Cement Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu and relied on State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai, Tilok Chand Motichand v. Munshi, D. Cawasji & Co. v. State of Mysore, Salonah Tea Co. Ltd. v. Superintendent of Taxes, and other authorities on discretionary relief and delay.

predicates.constitutional_levy_refund_claim: A party seeks repayment in a constitutional challenge to a state levy.
predicates.levy_is_declared_invalid: A court declares the challenged levy unconstitutional.
predicates.state_collected_cess_before_the_declarat: The state collected the cess before the court declared the levy unconstitutional.

issues.definition: When a court invalidates a levy, repayment is confined to collections made on or after the declaration rather than automatically covering earlier collections.

issues.legal_issue: An interim undertaking or direction cannot be read to require relief that conflicts with the final judgment.
material_facts: During the proceedings, parties gave undertakings and the Court made interim orders concerning collection, retention, or possible repayment of the cess.
The final judgment limited refunds to collections made on or after the relevant declaration of invalidity and provided for interest on those refunds.
issues.conclusion: The undertakings and interim directions did not require refunds beyond the relief allowed by the final judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Interim orders and undertakings must be read consistently with the Court’s final decision and cannot enlarge or contradict the relief ultimately granted. The Court applied this principle to the undertakings and interim directions recorded in these proceedings.

predicates.cess_validity_appeal: A proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a cess and seeks consequential relief.
predicates.interim_undertaking_or_order_addresses_r: A party gave an interim undertaking, or the court made an interim order, concerning possible repayment of the cess.
predicates.final_judgment_limits_refund: The final judgment restricts the scope of repayment.

issues.definition: When an interim repayment undertaking or order conflicts with the final limits on repayment, the final ruling governs.
